Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
# Review of "Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources"

This is a fair and well-proportioned synthesis. It accepts source 3's measurement corrections while rejecting its "entirely an artifact" conclusion. It recognises that source 4's "no decay" claim rested on uncontrolled studies, and it puts the coverage-bound result at the centre. Its main conclusion, that the answer depends on whether productivity is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output depends on presence, is right.

A few problems remain, and some matter for a policy audience:

- One of source 5's errors is carried over.
- One piece of arithmetic in Section 3 doesn't add up.
- The table doesn't show what the text says it shows.
- The briefing states the meetings mechanism more firmly than the evidence allows.
- Several open questions that matter to a working group are missing, above all cost and case backlog.

## 1. Errors carried over from the sources

**The decline from 12.5% to 8.5% compares two different measures.** Source 5's Summary made this mistake, and the briefing repeats it in Section 1. At nine months the 12.5% was measured against timesheet hours; the 8.5% at 24 months is against system-log hours. On the same timesheet measure, the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%. That is a decline of about a fifth, not a third. Either figure can be reported, but they shouldn't be compared directly.

**The per-worker result in discretionary work is described inconsistently.** Section 1 says source 4 found per-worker output "roughly maintained" there. That rests on the +0.6% estimate, which mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Source 4's own controlled estimate for discretionary work was −2.7%. Section 3 (point 2) gets this right, so Section 1 should match it.

**Source 3's novelty claim partly survives.** The briefing says source 3's "further claims do not survive later evidence." That holds for the "entirely an artifact" claim. But source 5 found the per-hour gain fell by about a fifth between 9 and 24 months, which is consistent with some novelty effect. What failed was source 3's claim that novelty explains *all* of the remaining gain. The briefing should say so.

**Source 4's "no decay" claim is better described as unsupported than "wrong."** One controlled study showing some decline doesn't establish how effects behave in general.

## 2. The per-worker arithmetic doesn't reconcile

Section 3, point 2, says that because actual hours fall 11–14% and output per hour rises 8–10%, output per worker ends up "around 2 to 4% lower." Multiplying the stated ranges gives a wider result:

| Per-hour gain | Hours change | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|
| +10% | −11% | 1.10 × 0.89 = **−2.1%** |
| +8% | −14% | 1.08 × 0.86 = **−7.1%** |

The 2–4% figure matches the *observed* estimates:
- Source 2: −2.1% at nine months.
- Source 4: −2.7% (controlled discretionary studies).
- Source 5: −3.4% at 24 months.

It doesn't follow from the reasoning given. Either cite the observed estimates directly, or widen the range. Both approaches should note that the confidence intervals reach about −8%. So "close to unchanged" is the central estimate, but losses of up to 8% can't be ruled out.

**The "four days" framing is misleading.** "Same output in four days" is not what happened. Actual hours fell only 11–14%, so staff worked the equivalent of about 4.3–4.5 of their former days. The accurate description is "nearly the same output from about 12% fewer hours."

## 3. Table 1 doesn't show what the text says

The table is labelled "ordered by strength of design," and the text says "estimates fall as designs strengthen." But:

- **The ordering is debatable.** The meta-analysis pooled estimate (+13.4%) includes uncontrolled studies. It is placed above the two uncontrolled subsets that use records and actual hours, which arguably have better measurement.
- **The figures don't fall steadily.** Reading down the table: 23.4, 11.8, 10.8, 13.4, 9.1, 9.6, 12.5, 8.5, 6.7. The 13.4% and 12.5% figures break the pattern.
- **The last row is a different kind of work.** Counter work (+6.7%) is coverage-bound. Ranking it last makes the downward pattern look stronger than it is, even though the low figure reflects the type of work, not the design.

Suggestion: split the table into discretionary and coverage-bound work. Within discretionary work, show the trend as uncontrolled with scheduled hours (+23.4%), then uncontrolled with actual hours (about 11%), then randomised (12.5% at nine months, 9.8%/8.5% at 24 months).

**"Converge on 8 to 10%" counts overlapping evidence as separate confirmation.** As I noted when reviewing source 4, its controlled, actual-hours, record-based and bias-adjusted subgroups largely contain the same studies. They agree partly because they overlap. The 8–10% range is probably right, but it rests on fewer independent results than the list suggests.

## 4. The evidence base is narrower than "five sources" suggests

The five sources are not independent:

- **Halden** data appear in sources 1, 3, 4 and 5.
- **Varden** data appear in sources 2, 4 and 5.

So the long-term randomised evidence for discretionary work, which drives the central estimate, comes essentially from **14 offices of one county government**. The briefing lists "private-sector controlled evidence is thin" as an open question, but understates the point. A working group should know the 8–10% two-year figure rests largely on one public employer.

## 5. The mechanism is stated too firmly

Point 4 says "about half the per-hour gain... comes from removing recurring meetings" as a finding. Several caveats from source 5 (and from my review of it) should go with it:

- **Mediation requires a strong assumption.** It assumes no unmeasured confounding between meetings and output, which a randomised trial does not guarantee for a mediator.
- **The trial has only 14 offices.** Treating office-months as separate observations probably makes the 28–66% interval too narrow.
- **The split is partly built into the measure.** If meeting time counts in the hours denominator, cutting meetings raises output per hour by definition.
- **The share could be much higher than half.** Source 5 doesn't say whether its log-in measure includes time spent in meetings. If it excludes meetings, the hours and meetings figures imply that almost the entire per-hour gain comes from removing meeting time.

Suggested wording: "In the one setting where it was tested, roughly half and possibly more of the per-hour gain appears to come from fewer recurring meetings."

This matters for policy. If meetings account for most of the gain, the question "is the hours cut necessary?" becomes the central one, not a side issue.

## 6. Open questions that are missing

These matter most for a working group:

- **Cost per unit of output.** None of the sources reports this, and the briefing doesn't derive it. With full pay and output per worker about 3.4% lower, labour cost per unit of output rises about 3.5% (1 / 0.966). Paid overtime would add to that; case-processing staff averaged about 3 hours a week of overtime. Lower sickness and turnover partly offset this, but by an unknown amount. For coverage-bound work, source 5 gives about +9% cost per contact to restore service. This is the figure a policy group most needs, and it should be stated with its caveats.
- **Case backlog and service in discretionary work.** If output per worker falls about 3% while cases keep arriving at the same rate, backlogs grow. Source 2 identified backlog beyond statutory deadlines as its key risk. Neither Varden report gave time-to-decision, so it is still unknown whether service in case-processing was maintained.
- **Sick-day normalisation.** If staff work four days a week, sick days per worker fall mechanically, because there are fewer working days on which to be absent. None of the sources reports absence per scheduled day, and Halden's 36% also compared against a seasonally different baseline. Point 5 calls the falls "real benefits." They are probably real in part, but their size is uncertain.
- **Possible bias in the Varden estimates:**
  - Two control offices cut their own meetings from month 15. This probably reduces the measured 24-month effect, and some of the apparent decline may reflect control offices improving rather than treated offices fading.
  - In the counter arm, if calls were routed between offices, the −11.4% may overstate the loss.
- **A reversion in discretionary work.** One of the three Halden organisations that reverted was a marketing agency, citing client deadlines. Source 4 would classify that as discretionary work. It is a single case, but it is the only discretionary reversion in the data, and Section 3 doesn't mention it.
- **Halden's attrition record.** Source 3 found that Halden misreported its withdrawals. Source 5, co-authored by Halden, doesn't correct this. A working group relying on Halden should know the original paper is uncorrected.

## Suggested bottom line

> In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours reduces actual hours by about 11–14% and raises output per actual hour by roughly 8–10% (best evidence: one randomised trial in public administration, two years). Output per worker ends up about 2–4% lower, though losses of up to about 8% cannot be ruled out, so labour cost per unit of output rises by around 3–4% before any savings from lower absence and turnover. In the one setting where it was tested, roughly half or more of the per-hour gain appears to come from fewer recurring meetings, which raises the question of whether much of it could be had without cutting hours. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added, at an estimated 9% increase in cost per contact. Untested: durability beyond two years, effects on case backlogs, private-sector and manufacturing settings, and whether reorganisation without an hours cut would produce similar gains.

The briefing's main contribution, separating per-hour from per-worker effects and discretionary from coverage-bound work, is sound. These revisions would make it more accurate on how much is known, and would add the cost figure a working group needs most.
